extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining patentability with respect to prior art (35 U.S.C. 102/103), including how to choose prior art, evaluate enablement/operability of references, and make appropriate rejections under AIA and pre‑AIA law.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103 (AIA) — Nonobviousness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained ... if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the differences between claimed invention and prior art would render the invention obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the effective filing date. Consider whole‑invention obviousness, not manner of making. See MPEP §§ 2131-2146, 2150-2159.04 for detailed guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103 (pre‑AIA) — Nonobviousness standard (pre‑AIA law)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained ... if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For applications/patents subject to pre‑AIA law, apply the time‑of‑invention obviousness standard. See MPEP §§ 2131-2146 for pre‑AIA analysis and any differing procedures. Use appropriate form paragraphs to indicate law applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnological process special rule (35 U.S.C. 103(b) / election procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding subsection (a), upon timely election by the applicant to proceed under this subsection, a biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter that is novel under section 102 and nonobvious under subsection (a) shall be considered nonobvious if (A) claims to the process and the composition of matter are contained in either the same application or in separate applications having the same effective filing date; and (B) the composition of matter, and the process at the time it was invented, were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If election is timely, treat the process as nonobvious when criteria A and B are met. A patent on the process must also contain claims to the composition or expire coextensively if composition claimed elsewhere. Define 'biotechnological process' per statute (genetic alteration, cell fusion, or using product of such processes). Follow statutory ownership/assignment rules when applying this subsection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of prior art — confine rejections to best available art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art rejections should ordinarily be confined strictly to the best available art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exceptions only where appropriate (e.g., peculiar claim interpretation, prior art that does not disclose inventive concept, AIA attribution exceptions under 37 CFR 1.130, pre‑AIA disqualification issues). Back up primary rejections with best backup obviousness/other art rejections (avoid merely cumulative rejections). See MPEP § 707.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to rely on abstracts vs underlying full text (foreign language) documents
rubrics_metrics.description: When both an abstract and the underlying document qualify as prior art, the underlying document should normally be used to support a rejection. When an abstract is used, the evidence relied upon is the facts contained in the abstract, not additional facts in the underlying full text. If underlying document is not in English, obtain a translation so record is clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain and analyze full text at earliest practicable time. If relying on an abstract only in a non‑final action, supply full text/translation in next Office action. Examiners may rely on machine translations unless quality is insufficient; applicant requests for human translation should be granted if supported by evidence the machine translation is inaccurate. See In re Orbital Technologies Corp. and MPEP § 901.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) and 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: For anticipation under 102, the reference must teach every aspect of the claimed invention either explicitly or impliedly; any feature not directly taught must be inherently present. For 103, the reference teachings may be modified to meet the claims and the modification must have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply strict element‑by‑element comparison for 102 anticipation; for 103, evaluate what a POSITA would find obvious in view of the combined teachings of the prior art and common knowledge. See MPEP §§ 2131-2146, 2150-2159.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine correct statutory subsection and effective filing/reference dates for 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to determine which paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 102 applies, the effective filing date of each claimed invention must be determined and compared with the date of the reference. The examiner must also determine the issue or publication date of the reference so that a proper comparison between the application and reference dates can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP §§ 2139.01, 2152.01 for effective filing date determination and MPEP §§ 2124, 2126, 2128‑2128.02, 2152.02‑2154.02(c) for reference date determination. Use form paragraphs 7.03.aia or 7.03.fti to indicate which prior art regime applies and follow MPEP § 2152.05 for choosing between 102(a)(1) and (a)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection by persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art, or by amending the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art. Additional ways depend on whether claims are subject to AIA first‑inventor‑to‑file or pre‑AIA provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to MPEP § 2152.06 for AIA 102(a)(1)/(a)(2) and MPEP §§ 2132.01, 2133.02(a), 2136.05 et seq. for pre‑AIA 102(a),(b),(e) strategies. Consider invoking statutory exceptions, affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.130/1.131 where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use/on sale/knowledge by others (102(a)(1) and pre‑AIA 102(a)/(b)) — evidence and procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An issue of public use, on sale activity, or other public availability can preclude patentability. Applicant may make admissions or submit sales evidence; examiner may have personal knowledge. If activity is by an entity other than inventor, pre‑AIA 102(a)/(b) may apply. If activity within the critical year, pre‑AIA 102(a) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If insufficient information, make a requirement for more information (form paragraphs 7.104.aia or 7.104.fti). Restrict questions to what is reasonably necessary (35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.104(a)(2)). Set a two‑month reply period (or SSP if applicable); failure to reply may result in abandonment (35 U.S.C. 133). Use form paragraph guidance and follow MPEP § 2133.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art presumed operable/enabling where it expressly anticipates or makes obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: When the reference relied on expressly anticipates or makes obvious all of the elements of the claimed invention, the reference is presumed to be operable. Once such a reference is found, the burden is on applicant to rebut the presumption of operability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a proper prima facie case of anticipation with adequate notice under § 132. Applicant may submit rebuttal evidence of non‑enablement. See In re Sasse and In re Antor Media Corp.; see MPEP § 716.07 for rebuttal/inquiry standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging enablement of a cited prior art reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a reference appears not to be enabling on its face, an applicant may successfully challenge the cited prior art for lack of enablement by argument without supporting evidence in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case law (e.g., In re Morsa) to evaluate whether argument suffices or evidentiary proof is required. Consider obtaining or citing secondary evidence showing how to practice the invention if primary reference is non‑enabling. See MPEP § 716.07.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement for prior art does not depend on type of prior art document
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of disclosure required within a reference to make it an 'enabling disclosure' is the same no matter what type of prior art is at issue (U.S. patent, foreign patent, printed publication, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not discriminate between references on basis of nationality or document type. Apply same enabling disclosure test across all prior art. See In re Moreton and MPEP § 2121.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacy/utility not required in prior art for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference must identically disclose the claimed compound, but no utility need be disclosed by the reference for it to be anticipatory; proof of efficacy is not required for a prior art reference to be enabling for purposes of anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on whether the compound/structure and method of making are taught or inherent; utility omission does not preclude anticipation. See In re Schoenwald, Impax Labs. v. Aventis Pharm., and MPEP § 2122.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of secondary evidence to show a primary reference is enabling (35 U.S.C. 102 rejections)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible to make a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection even if the reference does not itself teach how to practice the invention; secondary evidence (other patents/publications) can be cited to show public possession of the method of making the article or using the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite secondary references to supply missing practical details that would place the invention in public possession. See In re Donohue and MPEP § 2131.01 for procedures on using secondary references to show enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperative prior art may still be used for obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a reference discloses an inoperative device, it is prior art for all that it teaches; a non‑enabling or inoperative reference may qualify as prior art for the purpose of determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss references as irrelevant to obviousness merely because they may be inoperative; consider their teachings for combination or motivation. See Beckman Instruments v. LKB Produkter AB and Symbol Techs. v. Opticon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds/compositions enabling prior art — ability to make/synthesize
rubrics_metrics.description: One of ordinary skill in the art must be able to make or synthesize the compound; mere naming of a compound in a reference without a process or enabling disclosure cannot constitute a description of the compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the process for making the compound was not known at the relevant time, applicant must provide evidence. Evidence that attempts to prepare the compound were unsuccessful before the relevant time can show inoperability (In re Wiggins). The mere fact an author did not attempt synthesis is insufficient (In re Donohue) unless evidence shows no known methods existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds — unsuccessful prior attempts can show non‑enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference does not contain an 'enabling disclosure' if attempts at making the compound or composition were unsuccessful before the relevant time; evidence of unsuccessful attempts is adequate to show inoperability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may submit affidavits/declarations showing failed attempts. Compare In re Wiggins (unsuccessful attempts overcome reference) with In re Donohue (author not attempting synthesis was immaterial where synthesis methods were known). Consider practical impossibility of proving all known methods incapable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant genetics — enabling prior art requires ability to grow and reproduce the plant
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims are drawn to plants, the reference, combined with knowledge in the prior art, must enable one of ordinary skill to reproduce the plant; possession via publication plus ability to obtain plant (e.g., seed sale) and asexual reproducibility may create a statutory bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether publication identifies the plant, whether foreign sales put POSITA in possession, and whether asexual reproduction is possible without undue experimentation. Distinguish cases where only picture was published vs where seeds were commercially available. See In re LeGrice, Ex parte Thomson, In re Elsner, and MPEP § 2152.02(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus and articles — pictures/drawings may be enabling
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures and drawings may be sufficiently enabling to put the public in possession of the article pictured and may be used to reject claims to the article, but the picture must show all the claimed structural features and how they are put together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use drawings as prior art where they disclose all structural elements and assembly (In re Bager). See MPEP § 2125 for drawings as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art broad disclosure and nonpreferred/alternative embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are relevant as prior art for all they contain — not limited to what patentees describe as their own invention. A reference may be relied upon for all it would have reasonably suggested to one having ordinary skill, including nonpreferred embodiments. Teaching away does not necessarily vitiate disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not limit reliance to preferred embodiments; consider reasonably suggested alternatives and optional features. Cases (In re Heck, Merck v. Biocraft, Upsher‑Smith v. Pamlab, Celeritas v. Rockwell) support relying on nonpreferred/alternative embodiments. See MPEP §§ 2131.05 and 2145 for teachings away analysis in anticipation and obviousness contexts.
